# Chapters 1-3

## About

This page summarizes work related to chapters 1-3 of *Statistical Rethinking* [-@McElreath2020-fg].

## Setup

Source key libraries for more efficient and readable code.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(rethinking)
```

## Components of the model

See [-@McElreath2020-fg pp. 32-35].

$$ Pr(W,L|p)=\frac{(W+L)!}{W!L!}p^W(1-p)^L $$ {#eq-cond-p-W-L}

The probability of $W$ and $L$, conditional on $p$ is defined by the formula in @eq-cond-p-W-L.

The `dbinom()` function computes this binomial probability.
To compute the probability of observing $x=6$ $W$s in 9 globe tosses with $p=4$, we proceed as indicated below:

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| code-fold: false
dbinom(x = 6, size = 9, prob = 0.5, log = FALSE)
```

So, to compute the binomial probabilities for observing all $n+1$ possible cases, we proceed as follows:

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| code-fold: false

# Generate the data
n_W <- 0:9
p_n <- purrr::map(n_W, dbinom, size = 9, prob = 0.5, log = FALSE) |>
  purrr::list_c()

like_1 <- data.frame(n_obs = n_W, p_n = p_n)

# Plot the data
like_1 |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = n_obs, y = p_n)) +
  theme_classic()
```

To produce a set of binomial plots based on increasing numbers of samples, we proceed as follows.

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| code-fold: false

# Generate the data
n_samples <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64)

how_many_W <- function(n) 0:n
n_W <- purrr::map(n_samples, how_many_W) |>
  purrr::list_c()

n_states <- rep(n_samples, n_samples + 1)

p_n <- purrr::map2(n_W, n_states, dbinom, prob = 0.5, log = FALSE) |>
  purrr::list_c()

like_2 <- data.frame(n_states = n_states, n_W = n_W, p_n = p_n)
```

```{r}
like_2 |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = n_W, y = p_n)) +
  facet_wrap(n_states, ncol = 3) +
  theme_classic() +
  ggtitle("Probability density as number of samples increases.")
```

So, this figure isn't quite what I want. But it's a start.
What I think I want is a graph that plots the proportion of times $W$ was picked out of $n$ samples vs. the probability density. 

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| code-fold: false

# Generate the data
n_samples <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64)

how_many_W <- function(n) 0:n
n_W <- purrr::map(n_samples, how_many_W) |>
  purrr::list_c()

n_states <- rep(n_samples, n_samples + 1)

p_W <- n_W / n_states

p_n <- purrr::map2(n_W, n_states, dbinom, prob = 0.5, log = FALSE) |>
  purrr::list_c()

like_3 <- data.frame(n_states = n_states, n_W = n_W, p_W = p_W, p_n = p_n)
```

```{r}
like_3 |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = p_W, y = p_n)) +
  facet_wrap(n_states, ncol = 3) +
  theme_classic() +
  ggtitle(
    "Probability density for a given proportion of W's as number of samples increases."
  )
```

Yes. That's it.

## Chapter 2 exercises

### 2E1. Which expression corresponds to the statement: *the probability of rain on Monday*?

$p(rain|Monday)$

### 2E2. Which statement correspondds to the expression: Pr(Monday|rain)?

The probability that is is a Monday, given that it is raining.

### 2M1. Plot grid appoximate posterior probabilities for the globe tossing model.

::: {.callout-important}
This code is adapted from p. 40 in *Rethinking Statistics, 2ed*.
:::

```{r}
o1 <- c("W", "W", "W")
o2 <- c("W", "W", "W", "L")
o3 <- c("L", "W", "W", "L", "W", "W")

grid_n <- 20
p_init <- 0.5
p.grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = grid_n)
prior <- rep(p_init, grid_n)

likelihood_1 <- dbinom(sum(o1 == "W"), size = length(o1), prob = p.grid)
likelihood_2 <- dbinom(sum(o2 == "W"), size = length(o2), prob = p.grid)
likelihood_3 <- dbinom(sum(o3 == "W"), size = length(o3), prob = p.grid)

unstd.posterior_1 <- likelihood_1 * prior
unstd.posterior_2 <- likelihood_2 * prior
unstd.posterior_3 <- likelihood_3 * prior


posterior_1 <- unstd.posterior_1 / sum(unstd.posterior_1)
posterior_2 <- unstd.posterior_2 / sum(unstd.posterior_2)
posterior_3 <- unstd.posterior_3 / sum(unstd.posterior_3)

plot(
    p.grid,
    posterior_1,
    type = "b",
    xlab = "probability of water",
    ylab = "posterior probability"
)
mtext("20 points")

plot(
    p.grid,
    posterior_2,
    type = "b",
    xlab = "probability of water",
    ylab = "posterior probability"
)
mtext("20 points")

plot(
    p.grid,
    posterior_3,
    type = "b",
    xlab = "probability of water",
    ylab = "posterior probability"
)
mtext("20 points")
```

Now, here's a version that uses a function.

```{r}
#| label: define-est_p_water-function
est_p_water <- function(obs, p = 0.5, n_pts = 20) {
    assertthat::assert_that(is.character(obs))
    assertthat::is.number(p)
    assertthat::assert_that(p > 0 & p <= 1)
    assertthat::is.number(n_pts)
    assertthat::assert_that(n_pts > 0)

    p.grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = n_pts)
    prior <- rep(p, n_pts)
    n_W <- sum(obs == "W")
    likelihood <- dbinom(n_W, size = length(obs), prob = p.grid)
    posterior.unstd <- likelihood * prior
    posterior <- posterior.unstd / sum(posterior.unstd)
    m_comment <- paste0(
        n_W,
        " water observations out of ",
        length(obs),
        " | ",
        n_pts,
        " points"
    )
    plot(
        p.grid,
        posterior,
        type = "b",
        xlab = "probability of water",
        ylab = "posterior probability"
    )
    mtext(m_comment)
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### 2M2. Assume a different prior for *p*.

::: {.callout-note}
This is why it was worth the time to create a function!
:::

We need to modify our function slightly.

```{r}
est_p_water_2 <- function(obs, p = 0.5, n_pts = 20) {
  assertthat::assert_that(is.character(obs))
  assertthat::is.number(p)
  assertthat::assert_that(p > 0 & p <= 1)
  assertthat::is.number(n_pts)
  assertthat::assert_that(n_pts > 0)

  p.grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = n_pts)
  prior <- ifelse(p.grid < p, 0, p)
  n_W <- sum(obs == "W")
  likelihood <- dbinom(n_W, size = length(obs), prob = p.grid)
  posterior.unstd <- likelihood * prior
  posterior <- posterior.unstd / sum(posterior.unstd)
  m_comment <- paste0(
    n_W,
    " water observations out of ",
    length(obs),
    " | ",
    n_pts,
    " points"
  )
  plot(
    p.grid,
    posterior,
    type = "b",
    xlab = "probability of water",
    ylab = "posterior probability"
  )
  mtext(m_comment)
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### PM3. Two globes, Earth with *p*(Water)=0.70 and Mars with *p*(Water)=0.

We want to compute $p(Earth|land)$.

$p(Earth|land)=\frac{p(land|Earth)p(Earth)}{p(land)}$

$p(land|Earth)=0.30$
$p(land|Mars)=1.0$
$p(Earth)=0.5$
$p(land)=0.5*p(land|Earth)+0.5*p(land|Mars)$

```{r}
p_land_Earth <- 0.30
p_land_Mars <- 1
p_Earth <- 0.5
p_land <- p_Earth * (p_land_Earth) + (1 - p_Earth) * p_land_Mars

p_Earth_land <- (p_land_Earth * p_Earth) / p_land
p_Earth_land
```

### 2M4. Card deck with three cards.

$c_{bb}\rightarrow{b,b}$
$c_{bw}\rightarrow{b,w}$
$c_{ww}\rightarrow{w,w}$

There are two events. One involves the choice of card, the other involves the choice of side.
So, the space of possible outcomes when the observer chooses one card is as follows:

$b,b,b,w,w,w$

$c_{bb}$ could produce the observed data (black side up) in 2 ways.
$c_{bw}$ could produce the observed data in one way.
$c_{ww}$ could not produce the observed data, so there are zero ways.

So, there are three ways the observed data could be produced. In two of the ways, the other side is black.
Thus, $p(other-side-black|observed)=2/3$

### 2H1. Pandas.

$p(twin|A)=.1$
$p(twin|B)=.2$

We observe a panda who gives birth to twins, what is the probability that the next birth will also be twins?
Species is unknown.

Species unknown and likely sampled in equal proportions means that $p(A)=p(B)=0.5$

Species A could generate the observed first birth in 1/10 ways.
Species B could generate the observed first birth in 2/10 ways.
We want the probability of observing two consecutive twin births, $p(twin*twin)$.

$p(twin*twin)=p(twin*twin|A)p(A)+p(twin*twin|B)p(B)$
$p(twin*twin)=p(twin|A)*p(twin|A)*p(A)+p(twin|B)p(twin|B)*p(B)$

```{r}
p_twin_A <- 0.1
p_twin_B <- 0.2
p_A <- 0.5

p_twin_twin <- p_twin_A * p_twin_A * p_A + p_twin_B * p_twin_B * (1 - p_A)
p_twin_twin
```

So, the probability that the next birth will be a twin, given that the first was a twin, $p(twin,twin)=$`{r} p_twin_twin`.

### 2H2. More pandas

What is the probability that the species is A, given that the first birth is a pair of twins?
In other words, what is $p(A|twin)$?

$p(A|twin)=\frac{p(twin|A)*p(A)}{p(twin)}$

$p(twin)=p(twin|A)*p(A)+p(twin|B)*p(B)$

```{r}
p_twin <- p_twin_A * p_A + p_twin_B * (1 - p_A)
```

```{r}
p_A_twin <- (p_twin_A * p_A) / p_twin
p_A_twin
```

So, $p(A|twin)$=`{r} p_A_twin`.

## Chapter 3 exercises

```{r}
#| label: code-3.27

p_grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 1000)
prior <- rep(1, 1000)
likelihood <- dbinom(x = 6, size = 9, prob = p_grid)
posterior <- likelihood * prior
posterior <- posterior / sum(posterior)
set.seed(100)
samples <- sample(x = p_grid, prob = posterior, size = 1e4, replace = TRUE)
```

### 3E1

How much of the posterior probablility lies below p = 0.2?


```{r}
sum(samples < 0.2) / length(samples)
```

### 3E2

How much posterior probability lies above p = 0.8?


```{r}
sum(samples > 0.8) / length(samples)
```

### 3E3

How much lies between 0.2 and 0.8, e.g., in the interval $[0.2,0.8]$

```{r}
sum(samples >= 0.2 & samples <= 0.8) / length(samples)
```

### 3E4

Twenty percent of the posterior probability lies below what value of *p*?

```{r}
quantile(samples, 0.2)
```

### 3E5

Twenty percent of the posterior probability lies *above* what value of *p*?

```{r}
quantile(samples, 0.8)
```

### 3E6

Which values of *p* contain the narrowest interval equal to 66% of the posterior probability?

```{r}
HPDI(samples, prob = 0.66)
```

### 3E7

Which values of *p* contain 66% of the posterior probability, assuming equal posterior probability both below and above the interval?

```{r}
PI(samples, prob = 0.66)
```

### 3M1

Suppose the globe tossing data had turned out to be 8 water in 15 tosses. Construct the posterior distribution, using grid approximation. Use the same flat prior.

```{r}
#| label: simulate-8-water-in-15
p_grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 1000)
prior <- rep(1, 1000)
likelihood <- dbinom(x = 8, size = 15, prob = p_grid)
posterior <- likelihood * prior
posterior <- posterior / sum(posterior)
set.seed(100)
samples <- sample(x = p_grid, prob = posterior, size = 1e4, replace = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-posterior-p-8-in-15
plot(
  p_grid,
  posterior,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "probability of water",
  ylab = "posterior probability"
)
```

### 3M2

```{r}
#| label: fig-posterior-dens-8-in-15
dens(samples)
```

```{r}
HPDI(samples, prob = 0.9)
```

### 3M3

>Construct a posterior predictive check for this model and data. This means simulate the distribution of samples averaging gover the posterior uncertainty in *p*. What is the probability of observing 8 water in 15 tosses?

See p. 66 for ideas.

```{r}
#| label: fig-posterior-check-8-in-15
w <- rbinom(n = 1e4, size = 15, prob = samples)
simplehist(w)
p_8_in_15 <- sum(w == 8) / length(w)
p_8_in_15
```

### 3M4

>Using the posterior distribution from the new (8/15) data, now calculate the probability of observing 6 water in 9 tosses.

```{r}
#| label: fig-posterior-check-6-in-9
w <- rbinom(n = 1e4, size = 9, prob = samples)
simplehist(w)
p_6_in_9 <- sum(w == 6) / length(w)
p_6_in_9
```

### 3M5

>Start over at 3M1, but now use a prior that is zero below *p*=05. and a constant above *p*=0.5...


```{r}
p_grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 1000)
prior_new <- ifelse(p_grid < 0.5, 0, 1)
likelihood <- dbinom(x = 8, size = 15, prob = p_grid)
posterior_new <- likelihood * prior_new
posterior_new <- posterior_new / sum(posterior_new)
samples_new <- sample(
    x = p_grid,
    prob = posterior_new,
    size = 1e4,
    replace = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-posterior-p-8-in-15-old
plot(
  p_grid,
  posterior,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "probability of water",
  ylab = "posterior probability"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-posterior-p-8-in-15-new
plot(
  p_grid,
  posterior_new,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "probability of water",
  ylab = "posterior probability"
)
```

```{r}
HPDI(samples, prob = 0.9)
```

```{r}
HPDI(samples_new, prob = 0.9)
```

The HPDI for the new prior is narrower than the one for the flat prior.

We can also evaluate this relative to the known value of *p*=0.7, as follows.

```{r}
w <- rbinom(n = 1e4, size = 10, prob = samples)
simplehist(w)
p_7_in_10 <- sum(w == 7) / length(w)
p_7_in_10
```

```{r}
w_new <- rbinom(n = 1e4, size = 10, prob = samples_new)
simplehist(w_new)
p_7_in_10_new <- sum(w_new == 7) / length(w_new)
p_7_in_10_new
```

The probability of observing the expected number of 7 waters in 10 tosses is higher (`{r} p_7_in_10_new`) with the more informative prior than with the flat prior (`{r} p_7_in_10`).

### 3H1

We load the data from the rethinking package.

```{r}
p_grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 1000)
```

Next, we plot the posterior.


What value of *p* maximizes the posterior probability?

```{r}
max_posterior <- posterior == max(posterior)
max_posterior_index <- seq(1:1000)[max_posterior]
p_grid[max_posterior_index]
```

### 3H2

```{r}
samples_boys <- sample(x = p_grid, prob = posterior, size = 1e4, replace = TRUE)
```

```{r}
HPDI(samples_boys, prob = .5)
HPDI(samples_boys, prob = .89)
HPDI(samples_boys, prob = .97)
```

### 3H3

```{r}
boys <- rbinom(1e4, size = 200, prob = 0.5)
boys_model <- rbinom(1e4, size = 200, prob = samples_boys)
dens(boys)
dens(boys_model)
```


```{r}
boys_df <- data.frame(
  data = c(boys, boys_model),
  model = rep(c("pred", "obs"), each = 1e4)
)

boys_df |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_density(aes(x = data, color = model))
```

The baseline model assuming $p(boy)=0.5$ is shifted to the left of the model based on the observed frequency of boy births.
Thus, the baseline model does not appear to be a good fit for the observed data.

### 3H4

```{r}
p_grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 1000)
prior_1st <- rep(1, length(p_grid))
likelihood_1st <- dbinom(x = sum(birth1), size = length(birth1), prob = p_grid)
posterior_1st <- likelihood_1st * prior_1st
posterior_1st <- posterior_1st / sum(posterior_1st)

plot(
  p_grid,
  posterior_1st,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "probability of a boy as firstborn",
  ylab = "posterior probability"
)

samples_boys_1st <- sample(
  x = p_grid,
  prob = posterior_1st,
  size = 1e4,
  replace = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
HPDI(samples_boys_1st, prob = .5)
HPDI(samples_boys_1st, prob = .89)
HPDI(samples_boys_1st, prob = .97)
```

The highest density probability estimate intervals are shifted to lower values.

```{r}
max_posterior_1st <- posterior_1st == max(posterior_1st)
max_posterior_index <- seq(1:1000)[max_posterior_1st]
p_grid[max_posterior_index]

```

```{r}
boys <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = 0.5)
boys_1st <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = samples_boys_1st)

boys_df <- data.frame(
  data = c(boys, boys_1st),
  model = rep(c("pred", "1st"), each = 1e4)
)

boys_df |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_density(aes(x = data, color = model))
```

The model assuming equal probability of a boy fits the observed data for first borns better than the model assuming equal probability of a boy in both 1st and 2nd births.

### 3H5

#### Modeling 2nd births

```{r}
girls1 <- as.numeric(!(as.logical(birth1)))
boys1 <- birth1
boys2 <- birth2
girls2 <- as.numeric(!(as.logical(birth2)))
girl_boy <- as.numeric(as.logical(girls1) & as.logical(boys2))
boy_boy <- as.numeric(as.logical(boys1) & as.logical(boys2))
girl_girl <- as.numeric(as.logical(girls1) & as.logical(girls2))
boy_girl <- as.numeric(as.logical(boys1) & as.logical(girls2))
```


```{r}
p_grid <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 1000)
prior <- rep(1, length(p_grid))
likelihood_girl_boy <- dbinom(
  x = sum(girl_boy),
  size = length(girl_boy),
  prob = p_grid
)
posterior_girl_boy <- likelihood_girl_boy * prior
posterior_girl_boy <- posterior_girl_boy / sum(posterior_girl_boy)

likelihood_boy_boy <- dbinom(
  x = sum(boy_boy),
  size = length(boy_boy),
  prob = p_grid
)
posterior_boy_boy <- likelihood_boy_boy * prior
posterior_boy_boy <- posterior_boy_boy / sum(posterior_boy_boy)

plot(
  p_grid,
  posterior_girl_boy,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "probability of a girl then a boy",
  ylab = "posterior probability"
)

samples_girl_boy <- sample(
  x = p_grid,
  prob = posterior_girl_boy,
  size = 1e4,
  replace = TRUE
)
HPDI(samples_girl_boy, prob = .5)
HPDI(samples_girl_boy, prob = .89)
HPDI(samples_girl_boy, prob = .97)

max_posterior_girl_boy <- posterior_girl_boy == max(posterior_girl_boy)
max_posterior_index <- seq(1:1000)[posterior_girl_boy]
p_grid[posterior_girl_boy]

plot(
  p_grid,
  posterior_boy_boy,
  type = "b",
  xlab = "probability of a boy then another boy",
  ylab = "posterior probability"
)

samples_boy_boy <- sample(
  x = p_grid,
  prob = posterior_boy_boy,
  size = 1e4,
  replace = TRUE
)
HPDI(samples_boy_boy, prob = .5)
HPDI(samples_boy_boy, prob = .89)
HPDI(samples_boy_boy, prob = .97)

max_posterior_boy_boy <- posterior_boy_boy == max(posterior_boy_boy)
max_posterior_index <- seq(1:1000)[posterior_boy_boy]
p_grid[posterior_boy_boy]

boys <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = 0.5)
boy_2nd <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = samples_girl_boy)
boy_1st <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = samples_boy_boy)

boys_df <- data.frame(
  data = c(boys, boy_2nd, boy_1st),
  model = rep(c("pred", "2nd", "both"), each = 1e4)
)

boys_df |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_density(aes(x = data, color = model))
```

```{r}
)
posterior_girl_girl <- likelihood_girl_girl * prior
posterior_girl_girl <- posterior_girl_girl / sum(posterior_girl_girl)

samples_girl_boy <- sample(
  x = p_grid,
  prob = posterior_girl_boy,
  size = 1e4,
  replace = TRUE
)
samples_boy_boy <- sample(
  x = p_grid,
  prob = posterior_boy_boy,
  size = 1e4,
  replace = TRUE
)
samples_boy_girl <- sample(
  x = p_grid,
  prob = posterior_boy_girl,
  size = 1e4,
  replace = TRUE
)
samples_girl_girl <- sample(
  x = p_grid,
  prob = posterior_girl_girl,
  size = 1e4,
  replace = TRUE
)

eq_prob <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = 0.25)
girl_boy <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = samples_girl_boy)
boy_boy <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = samples_boy_boy)
boy_girl <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = samples_boy_girl)
girl_girl <- rbinom(1e4, size = 100, prob = samples_girl_girl)

birth_df <- data.frame(
  data = c(eq_prob, girl_boy, boy_boy, boy_girl, girl_girl),
  model = rep(
    c("eq_prob", "girl_boy", "boy_boy", "boy_girl", "girl_girl"),
    each = 1e4
  )
)

birth_df |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_density(aes(x = data, color = model))
```

Based on the observed data, the sex of a second child depends on the sex of the first child. If the first child is a girl, there is a higher likelihood that the second child will be a boy. If the first child is a boy, there is a slighly higher probability that the second child will be a girl.
